# Joining Tables using dplyr {#joining-tables-in-r-dplyr}

## Introduction

In this chapter, we will learn to combine tables using different `*_join` 
functions provided in dplyr. 

We will use the following R packages:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
options(tibble.width = Inf)
```
:::








## Case Study

For our case study, we will use two data sets. The first one, `order`, contains
details of orders placed by different customers. The second data set, `customer`
contains details of each customer. The below table displays the details stored
in each data set.








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/join_data.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::








Let us import both the data sets using `read_csv`.

### Data: Orders








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
order <- read_delim('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/order.csv', delim = ';')
order
```

We will explore the following in the case study:

- details of customers who have placed orders and their order details
- details of customers and their orders irrespective of whether a customer has 
placed orders or not
- customer details for each order
- details of customers who have placed orders
- details of customers who have not placed orders
- details of all customers and all orders

## Example Data

We will use another data set to illustrate how the different joins work. You can
view the example data sets below.








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/join.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::








## Specifying keys with `join_by()`

Every join below matches rows on the `id` column present in both tables,
written as `by = join_by(id)`. Use `join_by()` (dplyr >= 1.1) instead of a
plain string whenever keys need attention:

- same name in both tables: `by = join_by(id)`
- different names: `by = join_by(customer_id == id)`
- multiple keys: `by = join_by(id, region)`

:::{.callout-tip}
## Audit habit

Before trusting any join, run `anti_join()` in both
directions (see Anti Join). Rows on either side with no match are data-quality
findings, not join errors — investigate them first.
:::

## Inner Join

Inner join return all rows from `Age` where there are matching values in 
`Height`, and all columns from `Age` and `Height`. If there are multiple matches 
between `Age` and `Height`, all combination of the matches are returned.








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/draw_inner.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::








### Case Study: Details of customers who have placed orders and their order details

To get data for all those customers who have placed orders in the past let us 
join the `order` data with the `customer` data using `inner_join`. 








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
inner_join(customer, order, by = join_by(id))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


## Left Join

Left join return all rows from `Age`, and all columns from `Age` and `Height`. 
Rows in `Age` with  no match in `Height` will have NA values in the new columns. 
If there are multiple  matches between `Age` and `Height`, all combinations of 
the matches are returned.








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/draw_left.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::








## Case Study: Details of customers and their orders irrespective of whether a customer has 
placed orders or not.

To get data for all those customers and their orders irrespective of whether a 
customer has placed orders or not let us join the `order` data with the 
`customer` data using `left_join`. 








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
left_join(customer, order, by = join_by(id))
```

## Right Join

Right join return all rows from `Height`, and all columns from `Age` and 
`Height`. Rows in `Height` with no match in `Age` will have NA values in the 
new columns. If there are multiple matches between `Age` and `Height`, all 
combinations of the matches are returned.








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/draw_right.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::








### Case Study: Customer details for each order

To get customer data for all orders, let us join the `order` data with the 
`customer` data using `right_join`. 








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
right_join(customer, order, by = join_by(id))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


## Semi Join

Semi join return all rows from `Age` where there are matching values in `Height`, 
keeping just columns from `Age`. A semi join differs from an inner join because 
an inner join will return one row of `Age` for each matching row of `Height`, 
where a semi join will never duplicate rows of `Age`.








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/draw_semi.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::








### Case Study: Details of customers who have placed orders

To get customer data for all orders where customer data exists, let us join the `order` data with the 
`customer` data using `semi_join`. You can observe that data is returned only for those
cases where customer data is present.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
semi_join(customer, order, by = join_by(id))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

## Anti Join

Anti join return all rows from `Age` where there are not matching values in 
`Height`, keeping just columns from `Age`.








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/draw_anti.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::








### Case Study: Details of customers who have not placed orders

To get details of customers who have not placed orders, let us join the `order` 
data with the `customer` data using `anti_join`. 








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
anti_join(customer, order, by = join_by(id))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


### Audit pattern: check mismatches in both directions

A single `anti_join()` shows only one side. Before trusting a join, check both:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# customers with no orders
anti_join(customer, order, by = join_by(id))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 49 × 3
      id first_name city      
   <dbl> <chr>      <chr>     
 1     1 Elbertine  California
 2     3 Daria      Florida   
 3     4 Sherilyn   Distric...
 4    10 Abigail    Texas     
 5    11 Wynne      Georgia   
 6    12 Pietra     Minnesota 
 7    13 Bram       Iowa      
 8    14 Rees       New York  
 9    17 Orazio     Louisiana 
10    18 Mason      Texas     
# ℹ 39 more rows
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# orders with no matching customer record
anti_join(order, customer, by = join_by(id))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 245 × 3
      id order_date amount
   <dbl> <chr>       <dbl>
 1   368 7/2/2016     365.
 2   286 11/2/2016   2064.
 3   309 3/5/2017     480.
 4   179 12/21/2016  2358.
 5   484 11/24/2016  1031.
 6   115 9/9/2016    1218.
 7   340 5/6/2017    1184.
 8   493 7/11/2016   1558.
 9   340 2/15/2017   2330.
10   235 2/27/2017    149.
# ℹ 235 more rows
```


:::
:::








In this data, 49 customers placed no orders — and 245 orders have no matching
customer record. Those 245 rows are a data-quality finding (missing or
mismatched customer data upstream), not a join mistake: an `inner_join()` will
silently drop them, and a `left_join()`/`right_join()` will carry them with
`NA`s. Decide deliberately which behavior the analysis needs.

## Full Join

Full join return all rows and all columns from both `Age` and `Height`. Where 
there are not matching values, returns NA for the one missing.








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/draw_full.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::








### Case Study: Details of all customers and all orders

To get details of all customers and all orders, let us join the `order` 
data with the `customer` data using `full_join`. 








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
full_join(customer, order, by = join_by(id))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

      id first_name city       order_date amount
   <dbl> <chr>      <chr>      <chr>       <dbl>

 3     2 Marcella   Colorado   8/31/2016   1150.

 5     4 Sherilyn   Distric... <NA>          NA
```

## Cross Join

`cross_join()` returns every combination of rows from both tables (a Cartesian
product), so it takes no key. Use it for grids — e.g. all size × color
combinations — never for large tables, since the result has
`nrow(x) * nrow(y)` rows.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cross_join(tibble(size = c("S", "M")), tibble(color = c("red", "blue")))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  size  color
  <chr> <chr>
1 S     red  
2 S     blue 
3 M     red  
4 M     blue 
```


:::
:::








## Try it live {.unnumbered}

:::{.callout-tip}
## Try it in your browser

Edit the code below and press **Run**. It executes entirely in your browser
via [WebR](https://docs.r-wasm.org/webr/latest/) — no R installation needed.
The runtime downloads once, on this page only.
:::

```{webr-r}
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
order <- read_delim("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/order.csv", delim = ";", show_col_types = FALSE)
customer <- read_delim("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/customer.csv", delim = ";", show_col_types = FALSE)
left_join(customer, order, by = join_by(id))
```
